task_row_model.query: Given k sorted input files totaling N elements on disk, how should I implement a stable external k-way merge that minimizes disk I/O while using bounded memory? Describe the in-memory data structure, I/O buffering strategy, how to preserve stability on equal keys, and the resulting time and memory complexity.

documents.content: Academic description: A standard in-memory approach for k-way merging is to maintain a binary min-heap containing the current head element from each of the k sorted inputs. Each heap entry is a tuple (key, file_id, sequence_pos) so that comparisons use key first and file_id or sequence_pos as a tie-breaker to preserve stability across equal keys. On each output step extract-min and replace it with the next element from the same file using a single replace-root operation; this yields one O(log k) heap update per output element. The heap therefore requires O(k) memory, and the overall CPU cost is O(N log k) for N total elements merged.

Engineering note: In practice disk I/O dominates. To minimize syscalls and small reads, allocate per-input read buffers of size b and a single output buffer of size b; read file data into each input buffer in block-sized chunks and feed the heap from those buffers. This makes reads amortized over blocks, reducing I/O overhead. Memory for buffers is O(k*b) plus O(k) for the heap and small control structures, so total working memory is O(k*b + k). Implement the heap 'replace-root' (pop then push combined) to avoid two log-k traversals. Be mindful of OS file-descriptor limits when k is large; use multiplexed FD pools if needed.

Background and commentary: External sorting and merging have a long history in database systems; some papers propose loser trees and selection trees as alternatives to binary heaps because they slightly reduce the number of comparisons per output. There are also case studies reporting different optimal block sizes depending on spindle speed and SSD characteristics. These system-specific details are often secondary to the core algorithmic fact that k-way merging reduces to repeated selection among k heads; implementation choices about buffering and comparator tie-breaking determine practical performance and stability.

task_row_model.golden_answer: Maintain a binary min-heap of the k current heads storing (key, file_id, sequence_pos) and use file_id/sequence_pos to break ties for stability. On each output do a replace-root with the next element from that file (O(log k) per element), giving O(N log k) time. Use per-file input buffers of size b and an output buffer to amortize I/O; memory is O(k*b + k).
